claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The low hardness and strength are caused by an absence or insufficient degree of nanoscale short-range ordering.
The low hardness and strength are caused by an absence or insufficient amount of coherent precipitates.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy is a single-phase solid solution with minimal inherent nanoscale ordering or precipitates.
Controlled thermomechanical processing can induce nanoscale ordering or coherent precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Minor alloying can induce nanoscale ordering or coherent precipitates in CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanoscale short-range order can act as a dislocation-pinning structure.
Coherent precipitates can act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Induced nanoscale ordering or precipitates increase the stress required for dislocation motion.
Increased resistance to dislocation motion raises hardness and yield strength.
Absence of nanoscale order and precipitates permits easier dislocation glide.
Easier dislocation glide favors ductility and machinability.
Modified CoCrFeNiTi containing induced nanoscale ordering will have higher hardness than the baseline alloy.
Modified CoCrFeNiTi containing induced nanoscale ordering will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
Inducing nanoscale ordering or coherent precipitates will reduce ductility relative to the baseline alloy.
The magnitude of mechanical-property changes depends on the degree, uniformity, and stability of nanoscale ordering and on processing parameters.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits a minor alloying modification while also requiring that the overall equimolar composition remain unaltered and limiting the hypothesis to equimolar or nearly equimolar material; no substitution scheme or modified composition is provided to reconcile these requirements.

The intervention explicitly seeks coherent precipitates, whereas the boundary says secondary-phase formation is intentionally avoided. Coherent precipitates ordinarily constitute a distinct precipitate phase unless the intended feature is instead a short-range-ordered domain.
The design says all samples are to be processed under identical conditions even though the modified set must receive a distinct processing route intended to induce ordering or precipitation.

Failure to produce the proposed nanoscale structures is labeled as falsification, but it would only show that the intervention failed its manipulation check; it would not test whether successfully induced structures cause strengthening.
